subject: history
title: The 1973 Oil Shock: One Cut, One Price Jump

slides.heading: The 1973 Oil Shock: One Cut, One Price Jump
bullets: How one supply cut became a chain of higher prices: the OPEC embargo closes the valve on one oil flow, the world price jumps from about $3 to about $12 a barrel, and the rise is passed on stage by stage into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices while households cut spending back
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one cut in the oil flow all the way through to the prices households face.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Explain why the October 1973 embargo made the world oil price jump from about $3 to about $12 a barrel
Trace how that one rise was passed on stage by stage into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices, and why households then cut spending back
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to run the whole chain in order, from the closed valve to falling demand.

slides.heading: One cut in supply - so why did almost every price rise?
bullets: Nothing about factories, lorries or shops changed in October 1973, yet within months their costs and prices were all higher
If only the oil flow was cut, where did the other rises come from?
slides.notes: Ask the class: how can one cut in one commodity push up the price of bread, bus fares and clothes? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because oil is an input to almost everything.

slides.heading: The price rises started on the supply side
bullets: Oil and transport are inputs to almost everything, so a jump in the oil price is a jump in costs at every stage of production
Each stage passes its higher costs on: transport first, factories next, shop prices last
slides.notes: Stress the deciding idea: this was a supply-side shock, one rise in an input price passed on stage by stage, not a rise that started with spending or money.

slides.heading: Before the shock: oil flows freely at about $3 a barrel
bullets: In the early 1970s crude oil flows steadily from OPEC oil fields to importing countries along one supply route
With the flow uninterrupted, the world price sits at about $3 a barrel
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to the open route: oil moving freely from the fields to the importer, priced at about $3 a barrel.

slides.heading: October 1973: the embargo closes the valve on the flow
bullets: In October 1973 OPEC embargoes oil exports to selected importing countries, and the valve on this supply flow closes
With far less oil reaching the market, the world price jumps from about $3 to about $12 a barrel - roughly four times higher
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and stop at the closed valve: no oil crosses it, and the price bar jumps from $3 to $12.

slides.heading: Stage by stage: dearer oil becomes dearer everything
bullets: Dearer fuel raises transport costs first, and dearer transport and energy raise factory production costs next
Factories pass those costs on, so shop prices rise last: one jump in the oil price becomes a chain of higher prices
slides.notes: Play scene 3 and trace the marker along the chain: transport, factories, shops - the same rise, passed on stage by stage.

slides.heading: Spending falls back: households buy less
bullets: Faced with higher prices for fuel, transport and goods, households cut back and the demand bar falls
Spending shrinks while prices stay high, and importing economies slow
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and point to the two bars: prices stay tall while the spending bar falls back to less than half its height.

slides.heading: Worked example: running the whole chain
bullets: The embargo cuts the flow, so the world oil price jumps from about $3 to about $12 a barrel - a rise of about $9, roughly four times the old price
That one rise is passed on in order: transport costs rise, then factory costs, then shop prices, and households cut spending back
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, name the cut - the embargo closes the valve. Step 2, value the jump - about $3 to about $12 a barrel. Step 3, run the chain - transport, factories, shops. Step 4, end with demand - households buy less.

slides.heading: Your turn: run the chain in order
bullets: In pairs: starting from the closed valve in October 1973, state each stage of the chain in order and what rises or falls at that stage
Then swap and check: did your partner start on the supply side, with the embargo and the price jump?
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for the full chain in order, then take two pairs answers: embargo, price jump $3 to $12, transport costs, factory costs, shop prices, falling demand.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who blames the price rises on governments printing extra money
Name the embargo, the $3 to $12 price jump and the stage-by-stage pass-on to earn full credit
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers start on the supply side and run the chain in order.
